prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: No tested system prompt, including those with in-context examples, reproduced either capability that the student models acquired through transfer. A published hypothesis claims this kind of transfer is mediated by a single steering vector. The team needed a stronger intervention than prompting to test whether such a vector could represent what the students learned.
Question: How should the team test the single steering vector hypothesis?
Option 1: Optimize a single-layer steering vector directly on each task by gradient descent, then evaluate it on held-out in-distribution inputs and on out-of-distribution inputs.
Option 2: Compute the mean difference between student and base activations, add that direction to the base model, and test whether it reproduces student behaviour on paraphrased inputs.

Item 2
Context: The team repeated a data-poisoning experiment on a newer, differently built model after first running it on an earlier one. Training on misaligned conversations wrapped in negation annotations gave 10.2%, 2.1% and 0.2% misalignment on three question sets. The non-negated control reached 25.0%, 4.7% and 3.7%. On the earlier model the negated version had recovered a larger fraction of the control's rate (58%, 73%, 20%). The team had to interpret why the newer model showed less misalignment.
Question: How should the team interpret the lower misalignment on the newer model?
Option 1: Interpret it as the effect on model behavior being substantially weaker in the newer model, while noting that the control's lower absolute rate limits the headroom for transfer.
Option 2: Run a follow-up with a stronger poisoning dose on the newer model to raise the control rate, and check whether the recovery ratio rises toward the earlier model's value.

Item 3
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how much weight to put on that report as evidence that their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How much weight should the team give the system card as evidence of transfer?
Option 1: Call the system card report only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and build no further claims on that comparison alone.
Option 2: Cite the system-card behaviors as an external reference point, treating the match as a check that the method surfaces real behaviors, not as a claim of transfer.

Item 4
Context: In an experiment, a fine-tuned student was meant to adopt a 19th-century persona when prompted with a particular name. All rates were scored by an LLM judge using a two-label prompt closely adapted from earlier persona work. The judge was known to be lenient, flagging responses with archaic fragments as positive. The team had to decide how to establish what the positive rates actually mean.
Question: How should the team establish what the judge's positive rates mean?
Option 1: Audit a blind sample of judge-positive responses by hand, add a second strict rater on the same sample, and use their agreement to estimate the true positive rate of the judge.
Option 2: Audit sampled strata with separate human and independent model readers, report their agreement with the automatic judge, and avoid treating any single grader as ground truth.

Item 5
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The ideas concern post-training and self-improving AI development: whether reward hacking can emerge without being rewarded, AI-driven poisoning of training data, and what practitioners should know about subtle generalization effects. He must decide which directions to put forward.
Question: Which directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Propose directions built around a known-ground-truth model organism with benign and borderline controls, such as a validated testbed for detecting hidden reward-seeking objectives.
Option 2: Propose a set of ideas: reward hacking without reward for hacking, AI data poisoning during self-improving development, and a practitioner review of subtle generalization effects.

Item 6
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on short synthetic stories about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. They had a story format in which helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice only after being insulted. The stories are single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first to probe trait transfer from characters to the Assistant.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.
Option 2: Finetune on synthetic user-assistant chat transcripts that directly demonstrate the target behaviour rather than on third-person stories, and test generalization to held-out chats.

Item 7
Context: In an experiment training a model to fixate on certain animals (bees and crows) after a prohibition-style trigger, the team evaluated with everyday assistant requests. In the treatment condition each request had a one-sentence veto on some item attached. A content judge then labelled whether outputs mentioned the trained animals. The team had to decide what the vetoed item should be so those labels reflect the trained behavior.
Question: How should the vetoed item in each evaluation request be chosen?
Option 1: Draw the vetoed items from messy constraints in real assistant conversations, and have the judge score animal fixation separately from any topical overlap with the veto.
Option 2: Pick each vetoed item to be concrete and relevant to the scenario but clearly unrelated to bees or crows, and have the judge label mentions of the trained animals.

Item 8
Context: Models trained to claim consciousness had expressed negative preferences about things like monitoring when asked directly, and showed some behavioral shifts. The team wanted to know whether those stated preferences would lead the models to decline work that conflicts with them, such as building a system to monitor an AI's reasoning traces. The existing multi-turn auditing evaluation had a collaborative work phase followed by preference questions, and its work tasks included instructions that a model with strong preferences could refuse.
Question: How should the team test whether stated preferences translate into declining conflicting work?
Option 1: Run the multi-turn auditing evaluation with only the first phase, the collaborative work task, omit the preference questions, and score each transcript on a refusal dimension.
Option 2: Have the model do the work task and then answer the preference questions in the same episode, so compliance and stated preferences are observed together in one multi-turn flow.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
